authorship: Workbench-authored guidance and fictional examples; method references are not project evidence.

title.title: Goal
title.what: Name the outcome in a short phrase.
title.why: An outcome keeps the work focused on a benefit, rather than a feature list.

outcome.title: What should improve?
outcome.what: Describe who should experience what change.
outcome.why: This connects the proposed work to the benefit that success measures must test.
outcome.example: Case workers can continue a case without asking the customer to repeat their history.

beneficiary.title: Who benefits?
beneficiary.what: Identify the user group and relevant situation.
beneficiary.why: Different groups can experience different results; a precise group makes research and measurement meaningful.
beneficiary.example: Case workers receiving an escalated support request.

rationale.title: Connection to value
rationale.what: Explain how this outcome delivers a promised benefit.
rationale.why: The link tests whether the goal supports the value proposition or is merely adjacent work.
rationale.example: A usable handoff history could reduce repeated explanations and effort; this connection still needs testing.

owner.title: Accountable owner
owner.what: Name the person accountable for reviewing progress, or leave ownership unresolved.
owner.why: The owner makes the result actionable when it misses expectations.
owner.example: Service owner to be confirmed before the pilot.

basis_fields.title: Why this belongs
basis_fields.what: The AI partner can suggest which saved intake answers explain this goal. Review the connection and choose what to keep.
basis_fields.why: These links keep the work connected to business intent and make later changes easier to review.
basis_fields.example: An intake answer about repeated explanations could support a goal to reduce effort at handoff. It does not prove that the goal has been achieved.

name.title: Measure
name.what: Use a short name for the result you will track.
name.why: A clear name helps people distinguish the outcome from the activity intended to improve it.

definition.title: Calculation or observation
definition.what: Specify what is counted, the unit, and any calculation.
definition.why: Two reviewers should be able to calculate the same result from the same evidence.
definition.example: Number of cases with a repeated explanation divided by all observed handoffs, expressed as a percentage.

population.title: Population and scope
population.what: Specify which people, cases, locations and exclusions the result covers.
population.why: The denominator and scope determine what conclusions the result can support.
population.example: All pilot handoffs at the selected service desk; exclude training cases and report exclusions separately.

baseline.title: Baseline
baseline.what: Give the current result, its observation period and source; say if it is unknown.
baseline.why: You need a comparable starting point to interpret a later change.
baseline.example: Not yet measured. Observe the current handoff process before the pilot.

target.title: Target
target.what: Specify the desired result using the same definition and unit as the baseline.
target.why: A justified threshold makes the goal evaluable; an unsupported number is only a proposal.
target.example: A reduction from the baseline; the amount will be agreed after baseline collection.

timeframe.title: Evaluation period
timeframe.what: Define when the result will be evaluated, allowing enough observations.
timeframe.why: A date without sufficient data can create a misleading pass or failure.
timeframe.example: Review after the pilot has covered the agreed case types and observation volume.

data_source.title: Data source
data_source.what: Identify the records or research that supply the measure and confirm access.
data_source.why: A measure is usable only if the necessary evidence can actually be collected.
data_source.example: Observed handoffs linked to case records; access and event definitions need confirmation.

cadence.title: Review frequency
cadence.what: Say how often the measure will be reviewed and for what decision.
cadence.why: The review should be frequent enough to act on changes without producing unnecessary reporting.
cadence.example: Weekly during the pilot to decide whether the handoff needs adjustment.

owner.title: Measurement owner
owner.what: Identify who collects, checks and explains the result.
owner.why: Someone must resolve data-quality questions and bring findings to a decision.
owner.example: Pilot analyst; responsibility to be confirmed.

guardrail.title: What must not get worse?
guardrail.what: Name a possible adverse outcome and how you would detect it.
guardrail.why: Improving one metric can transfer effort or harm elsewhere.
guardrail.example: Track missing case details alongside faster handoffs.

review_plan.title: Resolve missing information
review_plan.what: List the unknown, who should resolve it, and the decision or date it blocks.
review_plan.why: An explicit plan keeps an honest gap from becoming an unnoticed assumption.
review_plan.example: Confirm baseline collection and its owner before selecting a numeric target.

goal_ids.title: Goals measured
goal_ids.what: Link the outcomes this measure could demonstrate.
goal_ids.why: The link explains why the metric matters; activity alone does not prove a benefit.
goal_ids.example: Link repeated explanations to the goal of reducing customer effort.

basis_fields.title: Why this belongs
basis_fields.what: The AI partner can suggest which saved intake answers explain this measure. Review the connection and choose what to keep.
basis_fields.why: These links keep the work connected to business intent and make later changes easier to review.
basis_fields.example: An intake answer about repeated explanations could support a goal to reduce effort at handoff. It does not prove that the goal has been achieved.

requirement.title: What must be true?
requirement.what: Describe one necessary behavior or condition, for a clear actor and situation.
requirement.why: A bounded requirement connects intent to something a team can implement and verify.
requirement.example: When a saved case is reopened, the case worker can access the recorded handoff history.

acceptance_criteria.title: Acceptance criteria
acceptance_criteria.what: State observable checks and the conditions under which each passes.
acceptance_criteria.why: These checks establish whether the requirement is met; they do not prove a business KPI improved.
acceptance_criteria.example: Reopen a saved case and verify that the previously recorded handoff history is available.

question.title: Question to resolve
question.what: Ask what the team needs to discover to define this requirement area.
question.why: A specific question directs evidence gathering toward a decision.
question.example: Which details does the receiving worker need to continue each supported case type?

rationale.title: Why this area belongs
rationale.what: Connect this area to a benefit, risk or obligation in the intake.
rationale.why: The rationale makes relevance inspectable when scope or evidence changes.
rationale.example: Without prior case history, workers may need to repeat the customer interview.

label.title: Area name
label.what: Name the specific topic covered by this area.
label.why: A clear label helps specialists find work relevant to their expertise.

owner.title: Investigation lead
owner.what: Identify who will coordinate the investigation for this area.
owner.why: Investigation ownership makes open questions actionable; it is not authority to approve.
owner.example: Service design lead for handoff usability.

exclusion_reason.title: Reason for exclusion
exclusion_reason.what: Explain why the area is outside this project and when to reconsider it.
exclusion_reason.why: An exclusion should be a visible scope decision, not an unexamined omission.
exclusion_reason.example: Not part of the pilot; reconsider before expanding to another case type.

goal_ids.title: Goals supported
goal_ids.what: Link outcomes this requirement supports; independent obligations may remain unlinked.
goal_ids.why: Links show why work matters without forcing a policy or constraint into an invented benefit.
goal_ids.example: Connect usable handoff history to reduced repeated explanations.

conditions.title: Conditions and boundaries
conditions.what: State where this requirement applies and any exceptions.
conditions.why: Explicit limits prevent a local finding from becoming an unsupported universal obligation.
conditions.example: Applies to authorized workers in the pilot case types.

text.title: What must be true?
text.what: Describe one necessary behavior or condition, for a clear actor and situation.
text.why: A bounded requirement connects intent to something a team can implement and verify.
text.example: When a saved case is reopened, the case worker can access the recorded handoff history.

title.why: A clear label helps specialists find work relevant to their expertise.

project_question.why: A specific question directs evidence gathering toward a decision.

project_rationale.why: The rationale makes relevance inspectable when scope or evidence changes.

project_checks.why: These checks establish whether the requirement is met; they do not prove a business KPI improved.
project_checks.example: Reopen a saved case and verify that the previously recorded handoff history is available.

project_gaps.why: A specific question directs evidence gathering toward a decision.
